## Programming Session {#sec-03-programming} ### Data Structures (continued) #### Factors Factors are used for categorical data - both nominal and ordinal ones. Factors are a special form of vectors: * Each element corresponds to a value from a set known as a factor's levels. * A factor's levels are stored in a specific order. ::: callout You can define a factor by using `factor()` command. For example, we have a variable measuring dose of vaccine administered (placebo, medium, high) in two waves of experiment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vec_1 <- c("High", "Medium", "Medium", "High", "High","Placebo","Placebo") fct_1 <- factor(vec_1) # Notice the difference in outputs vec_1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "High" "Medium" "Medium" "High" "High" "Placebo" "Placebo" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fct_1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] High Medium Medium High High Placebo Placebo Levels: High Medium Placebo ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # i.e., `factor()` creates a vector that contains two levels: "no" and "yes" class(fct_1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(vec_1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: Since these experiments were conducted in two waves. It could be of interest to denote the no. of wave for each experiment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Btw, table() command cn be used in R for cross-tabulations table(vec_1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` vec_1 High Medium Placebo 3 2 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(fct_1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fct_1 High Medium Placebo 3 2 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fct_2 <- factor(c("Run 1", "Run 2", "Run 2", "Run 1", "Run 2","Run 1","Run 2")) table(fct_1, fct_2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fct_2 fct_1 Run 1 Run 2 High 2 1 Medium 0 2 Placebo 1 1 ``` ::: ::: **Ordering Factors** Sometimes it is essential to specify the orders of your factor levels. Particularly during modelling and estimation with binary or categorical variables, given that the first level of factor is used in most functions, like `lm`(linear regression command in R), will be treated as baseline level or category. We use `levels()` within `factor()` command to do this. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Order is often determined using alphabetical variables by default) (H-M-P) # Ordering it fct_3 <- factor(c("High", "Medium", "Medium", "High", "High","Placebo","Placebo"), levels = c("Placebo","Medium","High")) fct_3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] High Medium Medium High High Placebo Placebo Levels: Placebo Medium High ``` ::: ::: ::: #### Dataframes In R, dataframes are data structure which store data in a tabular format. ::: callout We create dataframes using `data.frame()` command. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df_1 <- data.frame( Foo= 15:18, Bar= c(T, F, T, T), Name= c("Penny", "Sheldon", "Rajesh", "Leonard") ) ``` ::: Exploring the contents and structure of the dataframe ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Viewing dataframe df_1 # In Console View(df_1) # In Viewer # structure of dataframe str(df_1) # Names of columns/variables names(df_1) # Dimesnions of Dataframe nrow(df_1) ncol(df_1) dim(df_1) # Summary of dataframe summary(df_1) # See the output closely | very useful for understanding the dataset ``` ::: Accessing the objects inside dataframe ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Access Items using [] df_1[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Foo 1 15 2 16 3 17 4 18 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Access Items using [[]] df_1[['Bar']] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Access Items using $ df_1$Bar ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Access particular data point df_1$Foo[3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 17 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # what will be the output? df_1[1,3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Penny" ``` ::: ::: `Tidyverse` package has a very efficient framwork for working with dataset. Check the tidyverse book from day 2 for the same. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### [Exercise 1]{style="color:#1696d2;"} Let's go back and reload our sample dataset. 1. ## Conditionals in Base R Conditional statements let your code make decisions. ### Comparison operators (what they do) - `==`, `!=`: test equality / inequality (return TRUE/FALSE). - `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`: numeric comparisons. - `&`, `|`: logic operators - `!`: logical negation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 10 y <- 20 x == y # FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x != y # TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > 0 # TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x >= 10 # TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x < y # TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <= y # TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ### `if` - Runs a code block **only if** the condition is TRUE. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} if (x > 0) { print("x is a positive number") } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "x is a positive number" ``` ::: ::: ### `if ... else` - Chooses **one** of two paths. ```{{r}} if (x > y) { print("x is greater than y") } else { print("y is greater than or equal to x") } ``` ### Laddered `else if` - Chains multiple mutually exclusive tests. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # condition 1 x <- 10 y <- 20 # condition 2 x <- y # test if (x > y) { print("x is greater than y") } else if (y > x) { print("y is greater than x") } else { print("x and y are equal") } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "x and y are equal" ``` ::: ::: ### Nested `if` - Scope one decision **inside** another. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 20; y <- 10; z <- -30 if (x > y) { print("x is greater than y") #decision 1 if x>y if (x > z) { #decision 2 if x>y print("x is greater than y and z") } } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "x is greater than y" [1] "x is greater than y and z" ``` ::: ::: ### Multiple conditions and `&`/`|` ` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #one number x <- 5 y <- 3 z <- 1 x > y & x > z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #Vectors x <- c(10, 50, 30) y <- c(6, 40, 15) z <- c(12, 35, 40) x > y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y > z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > y & y > z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Descriptive Statistics & Aggregation (Base R) Summarize the [`mpg` dataset](https://rpubs.com/shailesh/mpg-exploration) to understand central tendency, spread, and relationships. ### Central tendency - `mean(x)`: arithmetic average (sensitive to outliers). - `median(x)`: middle value (robust to outliers). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Install if needed (run once): #install.packages("ggplot2") library(ggplot2) # loads ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr, tibble, stringr, forcats, purrr ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(mpg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` manufacturer model displ year Length:234 Length:234 Min. :1.600 Min. :1999 Class :character Class :character 1st Qu.:2.400 1st Qu.:1999 Mode :character Mode :character Median :3.300 Median :2004 Mean :3.472 Mean :2004 3rd Qu.:4.600 3rd Qu.:2008 Max. :7.000 Max. :2008 cyl trans drv cty Min. :4.000 Length:234 Length:234 Min. : 9.00 1st Qu.:4.000 Class :character Class :character 1st Qu.:14.00 Median :6.000 Mode :character Mode :character Median :17.00 Mean :5.889 Mean :16.86 3rd Qu.:8.000 3rd Qu.:19.00 Max. :8.000 Max. :35.00 hwy fl class Min. :12.00 Length:234 Length:234 1st Qu.:18.00 Class :character Class :character Median :24.00 Mode :character Mode :character Mean :23.44 3rd Qu.:27.00 Max. :44.00 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(mpg$displ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.471795 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} median(mpg$displ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Note: base R's mode() returns the storage mode, not the statistical mode. mode(mpg$displ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: ### Spread & quantiles - `var(x)`, `sd(x)`: variance and SD. - `quantile(x, p)`: p-th quantile (e.g., 0.25 = Q1). - `IQR(x)`: Q3 - Q1. - `range(x)`, `min(x)`, `max(x)`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var(mpg$cty) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18.11307 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sd(mpg$cty) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.255946 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(mpg$cty, c(0.25, 0.75)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 25% 75% 14 19 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} IQR(mpg$cty) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} min(mpg$cty); max(mpg$cty) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 9 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 35 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} range(mpg$cty) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 9 35 ``` ::: ::: ### Categorical summaries - `table(x)`: counts by category. - `unique(x)`: distinct values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(mpg$fl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` c d e p r 1 5 8 52 168 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} unique(mpg$cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 6 8 5 ``` ::: ::: ### Group-wise means (manual vs. `aggregate()`) - `aggregate(y ~ g, FUN, data)`: summary of y by groups g. - `subset =` lets you compute summaries on filtered rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Manual subsetting (repetitive) mean(mpg$cty[mpg$cyl == 4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 21.01235 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(mpg$cty[mpg$cyl == 6]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 16.21519 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(mpg$cty[mpg$cyl == 8]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.57143 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Using aggregate(): dv ~ iv aggregate(cty ~ cyl, FUN = mean, data = mpg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cyl cty 1 4 21.01235 2 5 20.50000 3 6 16.21519 4 8 12.57143 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Subset argument aggregate(cty ~ cyl, FUN = mean, subset = cty < 15, data = mpg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cyl cty 1 6 13.50000 2 8 12.05085 ``` ::: ::: ### Quick summaries (`summary()`, `by()`) - `summary(df)` gives per-column summaries. - `by(df, group, summary)` applies `summary()` within each group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(mpg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` manufacturer model displ year Length:234 Length:234 Min. :1.600 Min. :1999 Class :character Class :character 1st Qu.:2.400 1st Qu.:1999 Mode :character Mode :character Median :3.300 Median :2004 Mean :3.472 Mean :2004 3rd Qu.:4.600 3rd Qu.:2008 Max. :7.000 Max. :2008 cyl trans drv cty Min. :4.000 Length:234 Length:234 Min. : 9.00 1st Qu.:4.000 Class :character Class :character 1st Qu.:14.00 Median :6.000 Mode :character Mode :character Median :17.00 Mean :5.889 Mean :16.86 3rd Qu.:8.000 3rd Qu.:19.00 Max. :8.000 Max. :35.00 hwy fl class Min. :12.00 Length:234 Length:234 1st Qu.:18.00 Class :character Class :character Median :24.00 Mode :character Mode :character Mean :23.44 3rd Qu.:27.00 Max. :44.00 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(mpg$displ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu.
